prompt.context: Frank is 65 years old, and for his entire working career, has owned a manufacturing company which manufactures unibody car frames. He has always had one contract with one vehicle OEM, however this year that OEM has decided not to renew its contract.
prompt.question: What should Frank do?

clarifying_info.q: Why did the OEM decide not to renew the contract?
clarifying_info.a: A new type of welding technology is being used to make unibody frames, and Frank's plant does not support this technology. This new welding technology will soon be mandated for cars by a governing regulatory body.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of Frank's business?
clarifying_info.a: Frank's company is privately owned, 100% by him, with an annual contract revenue of $5M.
Frank has won numerous production efficiency and supplier quality awards. His supply chain is almost fully optimized, however he could source some materials elsewhere and save $100K per year.

framework: Value Chain Analysis: assess where Frank can gain advantages to lower his cost base or better meet customer demands — Design/R&D, Supply Chain Management, Production, Distribution, Customer Management
Profit Drivers: Revenue (can Frank find new customers, adapt his plant, or lease facilities?) and Costs (what will it cost to upgrade, manufacture other products, or acquire new customers?)
5 C's: Customers, Costs, Competition, Company, Context

questions.prompt: Should Frank upgrade his facility to adopt the new welding technology?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the upgrade cost vs. payback period. Frank requires a return on investment within 2 years. Upgrading costs $10M; current revenue is $5M with all-in costs of $4.5M (profit $0.5M/year). At $0.5M/year profit, payback would be 20 years — well beyond Frank's 2-year requirement. Even if Frank could save $100K in supply chain, profit rises to $0.6M/year, still ~16.7 year payback. Upgrading does not meet Frank's investment criteria.

math.setup: Upgrade cost = $10M. Current revenue = $5M. All-in costs = $4.5M. Annual profit = $5M - $4.5M = $0.5M. Possible supply chain savings = $100K/year raising profit to $0.6M/year. Frank's required payback = 2 years.
steps: Annual profit with supply chain savings = $0.5M + $0.1M = $0.6M
Both scenarios far exceed Frank's 2-year required return
math.answer: Upgrading does not meet Frank's 2-year payback requirement; payback is ~20 years (or ~16.7 years with supply chain savings).

questions.prompt: Can Frank find new customers for his current technology or his upgraded plant?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize two barriers: (1) Frank's current technology is being replaced by regulation, making it nearly impossible to find new customers for the old technology; (2) if Frank upgrades, potential new OEM customers have already signed long-term contracts with Frank's competitors. Neither path offers a viable new customer base.

questions.prompt: What are the strengths of Frank's company and can they be leveraged?
questions.guidance: Frank's strengths lie in R&D and design of unibody frame technology. However, the company does not sell anything else and has no high brand recognition or other expertise. Competitors have diversified portfolios, have all adopted the new technology, and have signed contracts with other OEMs. Frank's niche strength does not easily transfer to adjacent markets.

questions.prompt: What is the context around Frank's personal situation and what does it imply?
questions.guidance: Frank is 65 and would like to spend more time with his grandkids. He could consider lobbying the regulatory body for a freeze on the new technology requirement, but this would require a longer-term, dedicated effort inconsistent with his personal goals. His age and preference for retirement reinforce the case for an exit strategy over a turnaround.

brainstorming.prompt: Who may be potential buyers for Frank's business?

categories.name: Strategic Buyers / Competitors
ideas: Frank's underlying unibody frame technology may still be attractive to competitors in some ways
Competitors could acquire Frank's plant, equipment, or patents at a discount
A strategic buyer with existing new-technology infrastructure could integrate Frank's assets

categories.name: Financial Buyers
ideas: Private equity is probably not interested given the difficult growth story
Could be part of an industrial roll-up strategy of similar legacy manufacturing businesses

recommendation: Frank should exit the current market. He is the sole proprietor, quickly aging, and faces a contract termination that eliminates 100% of his revenue.
Frank should develop an exit strategy, which may include selling to a strategic buyer that can make use of his existing assets and/or has more patience for longer-term investments.
risks: If Frank closes the company, he must consider closure costs: long-term supplier contracts, outstanding debt, warranties, union fees, and potential ill will in the community.
Asset values may be limited if the technology is obsolete, reducing sale proceeds.
next_steps: Explore whether any current equipment or technologies can be adapted to make new products and assess the costs and revenues of doing so (initial signs suggest this will be difficult given the company's strengths are not in new technology).
Explore salvaging current assets and/or selling the business outright to a strategic or financial buyer.
